subject: Climate & Environment
title: Warmer Air, Heavier Rain
description: A 60-second lesson on Warmer Air, Heavier Rain.

hook.text: For every degree Celsius of warming, the atmosphere holds 7% more moisture. The math is simple.

buildup.text: More moisture means storms drop heavier rain. What was a 1-in-100-year event becomes 1-in-20.

discovery.text: Hurricane Harvey dumped 1.5 meters of rain on Houston in 2017 — a record for any US storm.

twist.text: Scientists found climate change made Harvey's rainfall 15% heavier and 3 times more likely.

climax.text: Cities designed for historical rainfall are flooding under storms their drains can't handle.

punchline.text: Warmer air is a bigger sponge — and it wrings out harder.

quiz.question: How much more moisture can the atmosphere hold per degree of warming?

details.summary: Warming air holds about 7 percent more moisture per degree Celsius, following the Clausius-Clapeyron relationship. This physical law means that storms in a warmer world produce heavier rainfall, increasing flash flood risk and total precipitation from major weather events.
details.whyItMatters: The 7 percent rule is one of the most robust predictions in climate science. It links every degree of warming directly to measurable increases in extreme rainfall.
takeaways: Each degree of warming increases atmospheric moisture by about 7 percent
Extreme rainfall events are already measurably heavier than in past decades
Heavy rainfall increases even in regions where total annual precipitation falls

faq.question: Has extreme rainfall already increased?
faq.answer: Yes. Observational records show that the heaviest 1 percent of rainfall events in the US have increased roughly 30 percent since 1958. The increase is consistent across continents and matches the Clausius-Clapeyron expectation.

faq.question: Why does heavier rain increase flooding even without more total rain?
faq.answer: When the same annual rainfall falls in fewer, more intense bursts, drainage systems, soils, and rivers cannot absorb or convey the water fast enough. Longer dry spells between rains also compact and seal soils, reducing infiltration capacity.
